components.description: Core problem framing: cross-agent noise limits cooperative MARL scalability

nodes.name: Shared return in cooperative MARL
nodes.description: All N agents share a single common reward/return, so each agent's learning signal is computed from a return that depends on every agent's actions.

nodes.name: Cross-agent noise
nodes.description: Because the shared learning signal depends on all agents, the stochasticity of other agents' actions enters each agent's own gradient/advantage estimate as cross-agent noise.

nodes.name: Cross-agent noise grows with N
nodes.description: The cross-agent noise term grows with the number of agents N, formalized as contributing O(N) variance to the per-agent policy-gradient estimator (Eq. 3).

nodes.name: Standard MARL is sample-inefficient at scale
nodes.description: Because variance scales as O(N), maintaining constant estimation error requires batch size to grow with N, making standard multi-agent policy-gradient methods sample-inefficient at large scale.

nodes.name: Classical credit-decomposition methods insufficient at scale
nodes.description: Counterfactual baselines, Q-factorization, and marginal-contribution estimation methods reduce variance somewhat but still extract signals from the shared return, so cross-agent noise still grows with N and eventually dominates.

components.description: Key insight: analytical reference models as a noise-free signal

nodes.name: Analytical models exist in engineering systems
nodes.description: Many cooperative engineering systems (cloud computing, power systems, traffic networks) admit differentiable analytical models that prescribe efficient system states (e.g., queueing models, power-flow equations).

nodes.name: Analytical prescriptions are system-level only
nodes.description: These analytical prescriptions describe system-level efficient states but do not by themselves yield local decision rules for individual agents.

nodes.name: Motivating question: converting system reference to agent-local guidance
nodes.description: The paper's central question is whether the differentiable structure of an analytical reference can be converted into agent-local descent directions that reduce cooperative policy-gradient variance.

nodes.name: Reference state and system state defined
nodes.description: A system state x_t (system-level quantities jointly determined by agent actions) and a reference state x̃_t (the analytical model's prescribed efficient state) are defined as the basis for guidance.

nodes.name: Localized agent influence on system state
nodes.description: Each agent's action typically affects only specific dimensions of the system state vector, so each agent's influence on the system state is localized.

components.description: Assumptions required for a valid reference/guidance signal

nodes.name: Exogeneity assumption
nodes.description: Assumption 4.1: the reference state x̃_t does not depend on the policy parameters θ (∇θ x̃_t = 0).

nodes.name: Descent-aligned reference assumption
nodes.description: Assumption 4.2: moving the system state toward the reference improves system performance, formalized as ⟨∇_x J(x_t), x̃_t − x_t⟩ > 0 for x_t ≠ x̃_t.

nodes.name: Reference need not be reachable
nodes.description: The reference x̃_t need not be attainable in practice (it may come from idealized fluid-limit or steady-state models); it is used only to define a descent direction, not as a literal target.

nodes.name: Valid, stable guidance signal
nodes.description: When Assumptions 4.1 and 4.2 both hold, the reference provides a stable, directionally correct target whose approach is expected to improve the cooperative objective.

components.description: Constructing the DG-PG guidance term and gradient

nodes.name: Deviation measure d(x_t, x̃_t)
nodes.description: A per-step deviation function d(x_t, x̃_t) = (1/2)||x_t − x̃_t||^2 quantifies how far the system state is from the reference (Eq. 6).

nodes.name: Reducing d is aligned with improving J
nodes.description: Under the descent-aligned reference assumption, reducing the deviation d at each step is directionally consistent with improving the cooperative objective J.

nodes.name: Deviation gradient decomposes per-agent via chain rule
nodes.description: Because d is differentiable in x_t and x_t depends differentiably on each agent's action, the chain rule yields a per-agent gradient term ⟨x_t − x̃_t, z_t^i⟩ that isolates agent i's contribution (Eq. 8).

nodes.name: Local influence vector z_t^i
nodes.description: z_t^i, the partial derivative of the system state with respect to agent i's action, is a purely local, analytically computable quantity depending only on x_t, x̃_t, and z_t^i (no other agents' stochastic actions).

nodes.name: Guidance gradient is noise-free
nodes.description: Because the per-agent guidance term ⟨x_t − x̃_t, z_t^i⟩ carries no dependence on other agents' sampled actions, it is a noise-free, analytically computable signal.

nodes.name: DG-PG gradient definition
nodes.description: The DG-PG gradient augments the standard policy gradient with the guidance gradient: ∇θi Jα = (1−α)∇θi J − α∇θi G, where α∈(0,1) is a guidance weight (Eq. 7).

nodes.name: Nash invariance (Theorem 5.1)
nodes.description: Under Assumptions 4.1–4.2, at any Nash equilibrium θ* of the original game, both ∇θi J and ∇θi G vanish, so the DG-PG gradient also vanishes for any α∈(0,1) — the augmentation does not create or destroy equilibria.

nodes.name: Standard PG variance is O(N)
nodes.description: The standard policy-gradient sample variance Var(ĝ_J^i) is O(N) because it relies on the shared return aggregating all agents' stochastic actions.

nodes.name: Guidance term variance is O(1)
nodes.description: The guidance sample variance Var(ĝ_G^i) is O(1), independent of N, because it depends only on agent-local analytically computed quantities.

nodes.name: Negative correlation between the two gradient components
nodes.description: Under Assumption 4.2 (descent-aligned reference), improving J reduces the deviation G, so the standard and guidance gradient samples are negatively correlated (ρ<0).

nodes.name: Agent-independent minimum variance (Theorem 5.2)
nodes.description: The minimum-variance DG-PG estimator (optimized over α) has variance σJ²σG²(1−ρ²)/(σJ²+σG²+2ρσJσG), which is O(1) since σJ²=O(N) and σG²=O(1) — breaking the O(N) scaling of standard policy gradients.

nodes.name: Optimal α shifts toward guidance as N grows
nodes.description: Since only σJ² grows with N, the optimal guidance weight α* shifts toward the guidance signal, satisfying α*→1 in the large-N limit.

nodes.name: Agent-independent sample complexity (Theorem 5.3)
nodes.description: Given L-smoothness and the PL condition, and using the O(1) minimum variance from Theorem 5.2, DG-PG reaches an ϵ-optimal policy in a number of iterations independent of N, versus O(N/ϵ) for standard multi-agent policy gradients.

components.description: Practical implementation and relation to prior methods

nodes.name: MAPPO advantage augmentation
nodes.description: DG-PG is integrated into MAPPO by replacing the standard GAE advantage with an augmented advantage: Â_DG^i(t) = (1−α)Â_GAE^i(t) − α·⟨x_t−x̃_t, z_t^i⟩ (Eq. 14).

nodes.name: Minimal computational overhead
nodes.description: The reference trajectory is computed once per batch from the analytical model, and each guidance coefficient is a simple inner product, so the added computational overhead is minimal.

nodes.name: No architectural changes required
nodes.description: Unlike COMA (requiring N separate critics) or QMIX (requiring mixing networks), DG-PG requires no architectural changes — only a single-line modification to the advantage estimator.

nodes.name: Cloud scheduling chosen as acute test case
nodes.description: Heterogeneous cloud resource scheduling with up to 1500 agents is chosen because queueing-theoretic priors are available and the cross-agent noise problem is particularly acute there.

nodes.name: Simulator induces prior model mismatch
nodes.description: The simulator's heterogeneous server efficiency, heavy-tailed bimodal workloads, and non-stationary arrivals violate the stationarity assumptions behind the queueing-theoretic prior, creating a deliberate model-mismatch stress test.

nodes.name: Mean-Field baseline excluded
nodes.description: Mean-Field MARL methods are excluded from comparison because they assume agent homogeneity, which the heterogeneous cloud environment violates.

nodes.name: Trade-off between α values
nodes.description: Across N=20 and N=50, larger α accelerates early convergence while smaller α achieves marginally superior best final performance.

nodes.name: Robustness to α choice
nodes.description: The small spread in final performance across tested α values (e.g., −8.75±0.21 at α=0.2 vs. −9.04±0.12 at α=0.8, N=50) shows DG-PG is robust to the specific choice of α.

nodes.name: Dynamic α schedule adopted
nodes.description: Based on the observed early-vs-final trade-off, a dynamic α schedule (starting high, decaying to 0.2) is used for N≤50, while a fixed high α=0.9 is used for N≥100 where cross-agent noise is more severe.

nodes.name: Comparable performance at N=2
nodes.description: At N=2, DG-PG, MAPPO, and IPPO all achieve comparable performance.

nodes.name: DG-PG outperforms at N=5 and N=10
nodes.description: At N=5, DG-PG reaches −10.97±0.38 vs. −21.63±0.77 (MAPPO) and −23.04±0.29 (IPPO); at N=10 the gap widens further (−9.69±0.23 vs. −29.40±2.07 and −28.71±2.81), despite MAPPO/IPPO receiving 2.5× more training episodes.

nodes.name: Performance gap widens with N
nodes.description: The performance gap between DG-PG and the MAPPO/IPPO baselines widens as N increases from 2 to 10, consistent with the cross-agent noise bottleneck predicted by the theory.

nodes.name: MAPPO/IPPO fail to converge at large N
nodes.description: MAPPO and IPPO are excluded from the large-scale scalability experiments because they fail to converge at these scales despite extensive tuning.

nodes.name: Scale-invariant convergence observed
nodes.description: From N=50 to N=1500, DG-PG reaches within 10% of its best observed reward in a bounded 6.8–17.7 episodes on average, with the required episode count not growing with N.

nodes.name: Empirical confirmation of Theorem 5.3
nodes.description: The observed scale-invariant convergence (P41) is presented as the empirical counterpart of the theoretical O(1/ϵ) sample complexity bound (Theorem 5.3 / P27).

nodes.name: DG-PG matches/surpasses centralized Best-Fit
nodes.description: DG-PG matches the centralized Best-Fit scheduler at smaller scales and surpasses it from N=200 onward, despite Best-Fit having centralized information and DG-PG being fully decentralized.

nodes.name: Decentralized coordination is learnable
nodes.description: DG-PG's matching/surpassing of centralized Best-Fit shows that decentralized, learned agent policies can achieve coordination comparable to (or better than) a centralized scheduler.

nodes.name: Bounded wall-clock convergence time
nodes.description: Despite per-episode training time increasing sharply with N (10.5s at N=10 to 335.0s at N=1500), the bounded episode count to convergence keeps total wall-clock convergence time moderate (under ~99 minutes even at N=1500), all on CPU-only hardware.

nodes.name: Learned policy is standalone at execution time
nodes.description: After training, each agent acts through its learned policy alone, without guidance or an online centralized scheduler — the analytical reference is used only during training, unlike residual-policy methods where the learned component stays tied to a base controller at deployment.

isolated_nodes.name: Difference Rewards require simulator access
isolated_nodes.description: Difference Rewards isolate per-agent marginal contribution via counterfactual simulation but require access to the reward function or a simulator.

isolated_nodes.name: Value decomposition structural assumptions
isolated_nodes.description: VDN, QMIX, and QPLEX factorize the joint Q-function under additivity/monotonicity assumptions and fail when the optimal joint value violates these assumptions.

isolated_nodes.name: COMA centralized critic requirement
isolated_nodes.description: COMA computes per-agent counterfactual advantages from a centralized critic conditioned on the joint action of all agents.

isolated_nodes.name: HAPPO sacrifices parallelism
isolated_nodes.description: HAPPO restricts agent updates to a sequential order so each agent can obtain a marginal advantage against fixed teammates, but this sacrifices parallel execution since each agent must wait for preceding updates.

isolated_nodes.name: Mean-Field MARL requires homogeneity
isolated_nodes.description: Mean-Field MARL replaces N-agent interaction with a population-level approximation, achieving scalability but requiring agent homogeneity, precluding heterogeneous settings.

isolated_nodes.name: Guided Policy Search / Residual RL limitations
isolated_nodes.description: Guided Policy Search and Residual RL derive a base policy from domain knowledge and optimize from there, but still suffer from cross-agent noise at large N, limiting improvement beyond the base policy.

isolated_nodes.name: Physics-Informed Neural Networks use prior differently
isolated_nodes.description: Physics-Informed Neural Networks encode prior knowledge as a loss constraint rather than as a basis for learning or an optimization direction, differing from DG-PG's use of prior knowledge as gradient guidance.

isolated_nodes.name: Cooperative Markov Game formalization
isolated_nodes.description: The setting is formalized as a Cooperative Markov Game / Dec-POMDP defined by the tuple ⟨N, S, A, P, r, γ⟩ with local observations and a joint action space.

isolated_nodes.name: Standard policy gradient theorem
isolated_nodes.description: Standard policy-gradient methods perform gradient ascent on the shared objective J(θ) via the Policy Gradient Theorem, using the sampled return R_t (Eq. 2).

structural_reasoning: The graph traces one dominant causal chain: shared-return cooperative MARL (C1) creates cross-agent noise that scales with N and defeats prior credit-decomposition and structural-simplification methods; this motivates using differentiable analytical reference models (C2) under two key assumptions (C3 — exogeneity and descent-alignment) to build a noise-free, agent-local guidance term (C4); this construction is what the theory (C5) formally certifies as Nash-invariant, variance-reducing to O(1), and yielding agent-independent sample complexity; the implementation (C6) shows this requires only a one-line advantage modification; and the experiments (C7–C10) empirically validate each theoretical claim in turn — robustness to the guidance weight, growing advantage over MAPPO/IPPO with N, scale-invariant convergence to N=1500, and a standalone decentralized deployed policy. The related-work critiques of prior methods (isolated nodes) and the base Markov-game/policy-gradient formalism are contextual/foundational rather than argumentatively chained to specific downstream result nodes, so they are listed as isolated nodes rather than embedded in the main components.
